payload.original: Historical investigation recorded from primary sources. Outcome: success. Apollo 11 lifted off at 13:32:00 GMT on 16 July 1969, the lunar module landed at GET 102:45:40 on 20 July after five computer program alarms during powered descent, and the crew returned on 24 July [A11-C001, A11-C066, A11-C073, A11-C076]. This investigation does not posit a failure: it examines why a complex descent continued safely despite operational anomalies.
payload.title: Apollo 11 lunar landing, July 1969: why the descent succeeded despite program alarms

payload.original: The Mission Report defines all times as elapsed time from range zero, the integral second before lift-off, and gives range zero as 13:32:00 G.m.t., July 16, 1969. [A11-C001]
The translunar injection maneuver ignited at GET 02:44:16.2, and trajectory parameters after TLI were nearly perfect (velocity within 1.6 ft/sec of plan). [A11-C004]
Lunar orbit insertion ignition occurred at GET 75:49:50.4, placing the spacecraft into a 60- by 169.7-mile lunar orbit. [A11-C005]
Undocking of the LM from the CSM is listed at GET 100:12:00 in the Mission Report sequence of events. [A11-C006]
After reacquisition of signal, Armstrong reported the LM undocked: 'The Eagle has wings.' [A11-C007]
Descent orbit insertion ignition was at GET 101:36:14 and powered descent initiation (descent engine ignition) at GET 102:33:05.2. [A11-C008]
The first program alarm (1202) is listed as computer-determined at GET 102:38:22. [A11-C012]
Armstrong reported the first program alarm on air-to-ground. [A11-C016]
Armstrong identified the alarm code as 1202, echoed by Aldrin, and asked Houston for a reading on it. [A11-C017]
CAPCOM Charlie Duke gave the Go on the first 1202 alarm about 31 seconds after the computer-determined alarm time. [A11-C018]
The second 1202 alarm is listed at GET 102:39:02. [A11-C013]
Aldrin reported the second alarm as the 'same alarm' and correlated it with having the Verb 16 Noun 68 display up. [A11-C019]

The ground's real-time response to the second 1202 report was an acknowledgment ('Roger. Copy.') followed by an offer to monitor Delta-H; the transcript shows no explicit 'Go' word for this alarm. [A11-C020]
The 1201 alarm is listed as computer-determined at GET 102:42:18, after entry into P64 at 102:41:32. [A11-C014]
Aldrin reported the 1201 alarm; Duke replied that it was Go, the same type. [A11-C021]
Two further 1202 alarms are listed at GET 102:42:43 and 102:42:58 (both computer-determined). [A11-C015]
For the later 1202 alarm(s) during P64, Duke acknowledged 'Roger. 1202. We copy it.' [A11-C022]
Program P66 (rate-of-descent mode) was entered at GET 102:43:22 to reduce altitude rate and keep height for site surveillance. [A11-C050]
Table 5-I lists the red-line low-level sensor light at GET 102:44:28. [A11-C057]
Aldrin called five percent fuel remaining and the quantity light at 100 feet. [A11-C054]
Duke called '60 seconds'. [A11-C055]
Duke called '30 seconds'. [A11-C056]

The Mission Report gives lunar landing at GET 102:45:39.9 (Table 3-I) and 102:45:40 with engine off at the same time (Table 5-I); Aldrin's 'Contact Light' call is at 102:45:40 in the ALSJ transcript. [A11-C066]
Armstrong announced: 'Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.' [A11-C067]
The Mission Report gives the commander's first contact with the lunar surface as 109:24:15 (9:56:15 p.m. e.s.t., July 20, 1969). [A11-C068]
Egress (hatch opening) was at GET 109:07:33 and ingress (hatch closing) at 111:39:13. [A11-C069]
CAPCOM Ron Evans passed the change to the crew: no rendezvous radar during ascent, to address the descent alarms. [A11-C082]
Aldrin told Houston from the surface that the rendezvous radar switch had been in Slew, not LGC, during descent. [A11-C038]
Lunar lift-off occurred on time at GET 124:22:00.8, into a 48.0- by 9.4-mile orbit. [A11-C070]
Docking occurred at GET 128:03:00; the rendezvous was successful with all guidance and control systems operating satisfactorily. [A11-C071]
Transearth injection ignition was at GET 135:23:42.3. [A11-C072]
Entry interface was at GET 195:03:05.7 and command module landing at 195:18:35, which the recovery table gives as 1650 G.m.t. on July 24. [A11-C073]
The crew, in biological isolation garments, were retrieved by helicopter to USS Hornet (crew aboard 1753 G.m.t., in the Mobile Quarantine Facility 1758 G.m.t.). [A11-C074]
The crew and spacecraft were released from quarantine on August 10, 1969, with no evidence of abnormal medical reactions; no microorganisms of extraterrestrial origin were recovered. [A11-C075]

payload.mechanism: With the rendezvous radar mode switch in AUTO or SLEW, resolver excitation came from a 28-volt 800-hertz supply frequency-locked but not phase-locked to the guidance reference; the CDUs slewed and sent continuous pulses to the computer (A11-C031, A11-C032, A11-C033). Repetitive jobs were then scheduled again before earlier copies completed, overflowing the Executive (A11-C029, A11-C030, A11-C034).
payload.statement: The 1202 and 1201 alarms were Executive overflows caused by counter interrupts from the rendezvous radar coupling data units, which stole more than 10 percent of the computer's capacity.
Crew monitoring displays (Verb 16 Noun 68) added computer load that reduced the remaining margin when the alarms occurred.
The alarms indicated a failure of the lunar module guidance computer.
The alarms were caused by a crew or checklist error in setting the rendezvous radar switch.

payload.mechanism: Mission Report: when capacity is exceeded the computer generates a software restart and an Executive overflow alarm (A11-C034); the alarms did not degrade any primary guidance or control function (A11-C035); participant analysis describes the restarts shedding load (A11-C046, A11-C047).
payload.statement: The computer's restart protection preserved guidance: each overflow triggered a software restart that discarded stale jobs and resumed the priority guidance and control computations.
Flight controllers could judge in real time that the alarms were not a guidance failure, because it had been decided before flight that such alarms would not prevent continuing, and they gave Go.
Armstrong's manual control in P66 extended the range past a boulder field around a large crater to a safe touchdown point.

The landing was completed inside the propellant margin, monitored in real time by the low-level light and ground callouts; post-flight analysis shows more margin than the real-time indications suggested.
Abort capability (abort guidance system, abort modes and mission rules) remained available throughout descent, so continuing did not commit the crew without a fallback.
The automatic descent would have reached a safe landing without crew intervention.

payload.mechanism: ANOMALY: counter interrupts from the rendezvous radar coupling data units, caused by unsynchronized 800-hertz excitation with the radar switch out of LGC, stole more than 10 percent of computer capacity (root cause of the alarms); monitoring displays reduced the remaining margin (contributing). CONTINUATION: restart protection kept the priority guidance computations running (enabling condition); controllers applied a pre-flight decision that such alarms did not stop the descent and gave Go; Armstrong flew P66 past a boulder field; propellant was monitored to touchdown inside the margin (contributing factors); abort capability remained available (enabling condition). The single assertion combines the anomaly and its successful handling because the v1 cause gate does not allow a second, independent assertion beside it.

payload.statement: Apollo 11 succeeded. The five 1202/1201 alarms during powered descent were Executive overflows caused by rendezvous radar coupling data unit interrupts that stole more than 10 percent of the computer's capacity; they did not degrade guidance or control. The descent continued because restart protection kept the priority guidance running, controllers applied a pre-flight decision that such alarms did not stop the descent and gave Go, Armstrong flew P66 past a boulder field to a safe site inside the propellant margin, and abort capability remained available. The real-time ascent workaround was effective.
